## The Research Loop, Assisted

::: {.three-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Find]{.card-title}

- Discover and track the literature
- Follow citations forward and back
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Organize]{.card-title}

- A private, searchable library of what you have read
- Search by keyword *and* by meaning
:::
::: {.card .card-teal}
[Write & review]{.card-title}

- Draft and edit with field-aware guidance
- Referee your own work before a journal does
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
Four moves, each with a tool you can install and use today. AI does the search, the recall, and the first pass; the judgment stays yours.
:::

## Literature Search {.section-divider}

## Finding and Tracking Work

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Ask, don't keyword]{.card-title}

- Describe what you want in plain language
- Discovery across [OpenAlex]{.accent} and [Semantic Scholar]{.accent} --- millions of papers, open metadata
- Get papers and abstracts, not just a list of links
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Follow the citations]{.card-title}

- What does this paper cite? Who cites it?
- Trace a result forward to its critics and back to its roots
- Surface the branch of the literature you were missing
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The web search from Day 2, pointed at the scholarly record. It finds candidates; you still decide what is relevant.
:::

## Knowledge Databases {.section-divider}

## Your Own Library, Searchable

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[What it is]{.card-title}

- A local, private store of your PDFs and notes
- Full-text keyword *and* semantic (meaning) search
- Import a whole Zotero library, or a folder of PDFs
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Why it helps]{.card-title}

- "What do I have on X?" --- answered in seconds
- Notes tied to the papers that prompted them
- Export BibTeX straight into your paper
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The `litdb` skill backs this --- your corpus first, external sources second. It runs locally, so your library and notes never leave your machine.
:::

## Writing {.section-divider}

## Drafting and Editing

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Field-aware help]{.card-title}

- Structure, argument, and clarity for an economics paper
- Synthesized from 50+ guides by working economists
- Section by section: intro, results, response to referees
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Sound human, not machine]{.card-title}

- Vary the rhythm; drop the AI tells
- Let the argument drive the structure, not a template
- Edit an existing draft, or draft from your notes
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The `econ-write` and `human-write` skills. They do not invent your findings --- they help you say what you found, well.
:::

## Reviews {.section-divider}

## Referee Before the Referee

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[What it produces]{.card-title}

- A rigorous, source-grounded referee report on a draft
- Separate editing notes and a prioritized revision plan
- The objections a real reviewer will raise --- first
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Others have built these too]{.card-title}

- Pedro Sant'Anna: a full paper-lifecycle suite, adversarial critic-fixer loop
- Lee Crawfurd: tightly-scoped review + replication-audit skills
- Installable, mostly economists --- Claude as [copilot, not pilot]{.accent}
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The `econ-review` skill does this for your own drafts. You own the question and the identification; the skill enforces the discipline.
:::

## The Risk That Matters Most

::: {.card .card-blue}
The biggest academic danger with AI is [fabricated references]{.accent} and claims a cited source does not actually support. The better research skills attack this head-on.
:::

::: {.three-cards}
::: {.card .card-dark}
[Verify every citation]{.card-title}

Checked against Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv --- bogus DOIs caught before export
:::
::: {.card .card-light}
[Audit every claim]{.card-title}

Does the source actually support the sentence? High-severity violations block the output
:::
::: {.card .card-dark}
[Flag contamination]{.card-title}

Detect citations that may themselves be AI-invented
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
For empirical or b-school research, this is the line between a demo and something you can responsibly put your name on.
:::

## Does It Actually Work?

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[The benchmark]{.card-title}

- 54 social-science papers, tested for whether a coding agent could reproduce the published findings from the paper alone
- Claude Code: [~93%]{.accent} at the individual-step level
- But only [~78%]{.accent} at the whole-paper level
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[What the gap teaches]{.card-title}

- It nails each analysis step
- One broken step anywhere still fails the full reproduction
- Exactly where human oversight stays essential
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The 93/78 split is the honest picture: extraordinary at the parts, not yet trustworthy end to end without a human checking the chain.
:::

## The Payoff {.centered-statement}

::: {.card .card-dark}
AI handles the [search, the recall, and the first pass]{.accent} --- finding the literature, remembering what you read, drafting the prose, refereeing the draft. You decide [what matters and whether it is right.]{.accent}
:::

## Breakout {.section-divider}

## Questions to Discuss

- Where in your own research does recall of the literature slow you down most?
- What would you keep in a private knowledge base that you would never put in a public tool?
- Which is riskier to hand to AI --- the drafting, or the reviewing? Why?
- Given the 93/78 result, which parts of your empirical work would you let AI run, and which would you always check yourself?
